source.lesson: none: a test and a reference for the kit (src/Kit/Kit.fs)

scenes.say: The stage kit gallery.
This gallery shows every piece of the stage kit. Each piece appears as the narrator names it.
Step one: text, lines and chips.
A heading sits at the top. Lines arrive with the words: first this one, then a second with a note, and a third that gets struck out. Chips appear one by one: accent, good, bad, and warn.
Step two: tables and bars.
A table fills row by row: the cache, the load balancer, and the queue.
Bars grow to their values against a capacity line. The database needs two and a half times its capacity, and the network eight times. Then the network drops back to one.
A table cell can also wait for its own word. The small plan serves one thousand requests for five dollars. The large plan serves ten thousand for forty dollars.
Step three: timelines and flows.
A timeline stacks its segments: thirty for the lookup, ninety for the handshake, eight for the work, and [308](three hundred and eight) in all.
A flow draws boxes, arrows between them, and packets moving along. The client calls the server, and the reply comes back.
An edge can choose where it meets a box. The service reads the cache from the left of its bottom side, and writes to the database from the right, so the two pairs never cross.
Step four: code, whiteboards and steps.
Code lines glow as they run: read, then handle, then commit.
A whiteboard types its working: fifty million times ten is five hundred million a day.
Steps light up in turn: find, then move, then price. And a counter counts up to three million.
Last: toasts, the small badges that flag a moment.

Here is a key idea. But here's the tricky part. Remember the offsets from before. Be careful with this setting. A common mistake is committing first. Surprisingly, reading removes nothing. A short note goes here. Ask yourself why that is. And a pro tip to finish.
A module can place its own toast too, with custom text, right where its content is.
Finally: breathing room, so a point can land.
A pause after a key point gives it a moment to sink in. [pause] Now a question for you: why does a pause help at all? [think 4] Because the viewer needs time to connect it to what they already know.

recap: A pause lets a key point land
A think gives a question its silence
scenes.say: So far: a pause lets a key point land. A think gives a question its silence. And a recap like this one closes each chapter.
That is the whole kit.
